sections.title: 01 Operating System Fundamentals
sections.description: Understand core goals, services, user interfaces, system structures, and kernel design architectures.

topics.title: OS Goals
topics.what_is_it: The three primary objectives of an Operating System: providing Convenience (user-friendly abstraction over hardware), ensuring Efficiency (optimal utilization of CPU, memory, and I/O), and enabling Hardware Abstraction (shielding applications from hardware-specific details).
topics.simple_explanation:
Without an OS, every program would need to directly manage CPU registers, memory addresses, disk sectors, and device controllers — making software development nearly impossible.

An OS solves this by sitting between hardware and applications:
- **Convenience**: You type `open('file.txt')` instead of sending raw SATA commands to disk controller at port 0x1F0.
- **Efficiency**: The OS multiplexes CPU time across 200 Chrome tabs, Spotify, and VS Code simultaneously using scheduling algorithms.
- **Abstraction**: Whether your laptop has an Intel i7 or AMD Ryzen, your Python script runs identically because the OS abstracts the hardware differences.
topics.real_world_analogy: An OS is like a hotel manager. Guests (applications) don't deal with plumbing, electricity, or room cleaning directly. They just call the front desk (system calls). The manager (OS) allocates rooms (memory), schedules housekeeping (CPU scheduling), and handles emergencies (interrupts) — all invisible to guests.
why_it_exists: Without an OS, every application would need to include its own hardware drivers — duplicating millions of lines of device-specific code.
Multiple programs running simultaneously would corrupt each other's memory without OS-managed address space isolation.
Hardware resources (CPU cores, RAM, disk bandwidth) need fair allocation policies to prevent one greedy process from starving others.
tech_world: Linux kernel provides hardware abstraction for 1000+ device drivers, letting the same Node.js server run on x86 laptops, ARM Raspberry Pis, and cloud VMs.
Android OS enables apps written in Java/Kotlin to run on Samsung, Xiaomi, and Pixel phones despite completely different chipsets.
key_points: Convenience: Abstracts hardware complexity behind simple APIs (file I/O, network sockets).
Efficiency: Multiplexes CPU, memory, and I/O across concurrent processes using scheduling and allocation algorithms.
Abstraction: Applications are hardware-independent — write once, run on any supported platform.
Resource Manager: OS arbitrates access to shared resources preventing conflicts and starvation.
Security Boundary: OS enforces isolation between user processes and privileged kernel operations.
interview_focus: Why do we need an operating system? What happens without one?
What are the primary functions of an OS as a resource manager?

interview_questions.question: What are the primary goals of an Operating System?
interview_questions.answer:
Three primary goals:
1. **Convenience**: Provide user-friendly abstractions (file systems, GUI, system calls) so applications don't interact with raw hardware.
2. **Efficiency**: Maximize CPU utilization, minimize I/O wait, and fairly allocate memory across competing processes.
3. **Abstraction**: Hide hardware-specific details behind standard interfaces, enabling portable software that runs on different chipsets and architectures.

interview_questions.question: What would happen if there was no operating system on a computer?
interview_questions.answer: Without an OS: (1) Each program must include its own device drivers for every piece of hardware. (2) Only one program can run at a time — no multitasking. (3) Programs can overwrite each other's memory — no protection. (4) No file system — applications must track raw disk sectors manually. (5) No networking stack — each app must implement TCP/IP from scratch. Embedded systems like Arduino demonstrate this: they run bare-metal code with no OS, limiting them to single-task execution.

topics.title: OS Services
topics.what_is_it: Core services provided by the OS kernel: Program Execution (loading and running binaries), I/O Operations (reading/writing devices), File System Manipulation (creating, deleting, navigating files), Inter-Process Communication (pipes, sockets, shared memory), Resource Allocation (CPU, memory, disk scheduling), Error Detection & Handling, and Protection & Security (access control, user isolation).
topics.simple_explanation:
An OS provides 7 essential services that every application relies on:

1. **Program Execution**: OS loads your `.exe` or ELF binary from disk into RAM, sets up the virtual address space (code, heap, stack segments), and starts execution at `main()`.
2. **I/O Operations**: When you call `console.log()` in Node.js, the OS routes output to your terminal device via the `write()` system call.
3. **File System**: `fs.readFile('data.json')` translates to the OS navigating inode tables, reading disk blocks, and returning bytes.
4. **Communication (IPC)**: Two processes share data via pipes (`ls | grep txt`), message queues, shared memory segments, or network sockets.
5. **Resource Allocation**: When 10 processes compete for 4 CPU cores, the scheduler decides who runs, for how long, and in what order.
6. **Error Detection**: OS catches division-by-zero (SIGFPE), segmentation faults (SIGSEGV), and hardware failures (disk bad sectors).
7. **Protection**: Process A cannot read Process B's memory. Regular users cannot execute `rm -rf /` on system files.
topics.real_world_analogy: An OS is like a well-run government providing public services: Transportation (I/O), Post Office (IPC), Land Registry (File System), Police (Protection), Census Bureau (Resource Allocation), Fire Department (Error Detection), and Employment Office (Program Execution — finding jobs for workers).
why_it_exists: Applications need a standardized way to perform I/O without knowing whether the storage is an SSD, HDD, or network drive.
Multi-user systems require protection services to prevent one user from accessing another's files or killing their processes.
Error detection at the OS level prevents a single buggy application from crashing the entire machine.
tech_world: Docker containers rely on OS services for filesystem isolation (OverlayFS), network namespace separation, and cgroup resource limits.
PostgreSQL relies on OS file system services for WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) and OS memory services for shared buffer pool allocation.
key_points: Program Execution: Load binary → allocate memory → initialize stack → jump to entry point.
I/O Operations: Abstracted via system calls (read/write/ioctl) regardless of device type.
File System: Hierarchical namespace with permissions, metadata, and block allocation.
IPC: Pipes, message queues, shared memory, signals, and sockets for inter-process data exchange.
Resource Allocation: CPU scheduling, memory allocation, and disk I/O scheduling.
Error Detection: Hardware errors (bad sectors), software errors (segfault), and resource exhaustion (OOM).
Protection & Security: Memory isolation, file permissions, and user/group access control.
interview_focus: Name the core services provided by an OS and give a real example for each.
How does the OS handle error detection vs error recovery?

interview_questions.question: What are the major services provided by an Operating System?
interview_questions.answer:
7 major services:
1. **Program Execution**: Loading programs into memory and managing their lifecycle.
2. **I/O Operations**: Providing uniform interfaces to diverse hardware devices.
3. **File System Manipulation**: Creating, reading, writing, deleting, and organizing files in a hierarchical structure.
4. **Inter-Process Communication**: Enabling data exchange between processes via pipes, shared memory, message queues, and sockets.
5. **Resource Allocation**: Scheduling CPU time, allocating memory, and managing disk bandwidth among competing processes.
6. **Error Detection**: Detecting hardware failures, illegal memory access, arithmetic errors, and resource exhaustion.
7. **Protection & Security**: Isolating processes, enforcing file permissions, and authenticating users.

topics.title: OS Interfaces
topics.what_is_it: The three primary mechanisms users interact with the OS: Command-Line Interface (CLI/Shell like Bash, Zsh, PowerShell), Graphical User Interface (GUI like Windows Desktop, GNOME, macOS Finder), and Batch Interface (executing pre-written scripts without user interaction).
topics.simple_explanation:
Users interact with the OS through different interfaces depending on the use case:

- **CLI (Command-Line Interface)**: You type text commands into a shell. `ls -la /home` lists files. Power users and DevOps engineers prefer CLI because it's scriptable, fast, and works over SSH on remote servers. Bash, Zsh, Fish, and PowerShell are popular shells.
- **GUI (Graphical User Interface)**: Point-and-click with mouse. Windows Explorer, macOS Finder, Ubuntu GNOME Desktop. Easier for beginners but impossible to automate or use over SSH.
- **Batch Interface**: A text file containing a sequence of OS commands executed without user interaction. Examples: `.sh` scripts on Linux, `.bat` files on Windows, cron jobs, and CI/CD pipelines. This is how production servers run automated tasks.
topics.real_world_analogy: CLI is like ordering food by calling the restaurant and speaking your order precisely. GUI is like browsing a visual menu at a restaurant and pointing at pictures. Batch is like writing your weekly food order on a paper and handing it to the delivery service every Monday morning.
why_it_exists: CLI enables automation: a 50-step deployment can be scripted into a single `deploy.sh` file.
GUI makes computers accessible to non-technical users who don't want to memorize commands.
Batch interfaces enable unattended server administration — cron jobs run backups at 3 AM without human intervention.
tech_world: Production Linux servers exclusively use CLI over SSH — no GUI is installed to save memory and reduce attack surface.
CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions, Jenkins) are batch interfaces that execute build/test/deploy scripts automatically on every code push.
key_points: CLI: Text-based, scriptable, works over SSH, preferred for servers and automation.
GUI: Visual, mouse-driven, easier for beginners, high resource consumption.
Batch: Pre-written command sequences executed without interaction (cron, CI/CD, .bat files).
Shell vs Terminal: Shell is the command interpreter (Bash); Terminal is the window application (iTerm2, Windows Terminal).
Modern trend: GUI for development (VS Code), CLI for deployment and server management.
interview_focus: Why do servers use CLI instead of GUI?
What is the difference between a Shell and a Terminal?

interview_questions.question: Why do production servers typically not have a GUI installed?
interview_questions.answer: Production servers avoid GUI because: (1) GUI consumes significant RAM and CPU resources (X11/Wayland display server, window manager, desktop environment) that should be dedicated to the application workload. (2) GUI increases attack surface — more code means more potential security vulnerabilities. (3) Servers are managed remotely via SSH, which only supports CLI. (4) Automation requires scriptable CLI commands, not mouse clicks.

topics.title: OS Structures
topics.what_is_it: The four primary architectural approaches for designing an OS kernel: Simple/Monolithic (all services in one kernel binary), Layered (organized into hierarchical abstraction layers), Microkernel (minimal kernel with services in user-space), and Hybrid (pragmatic combination used by modern OS).
topics.simple_explanation:
How you organize OS code determines its performance, security, and maintainability:

1. **Simple/Monolithic Structure (MS-DOS)**: No clear separation — application code could directly access hardware. Fast but zero protection. A single bug could crash the entire system.
2. **Layered Architecture**: OS divided into numbered layers (Layer 0 = Hardware, Layer N = User Interface). Each layer only uses services from the layer below. Clean design but high overhead from multiple layer transitions.
3. **Microkernel**: Only the absolute minimum runs in kernel mode (IPC, basic scheduling, memory mapping). Everything else (file system, device drivers, networking) runs as user-space processes. Very secure (driver crash doesn't crash OS) but slow due to frequent user↔kernel context switches.
4. **Hybrid Kernel**: Pragmatic compromise used by real-world OS. Linux is monolithic but modular (loadable kernel modules). Windows NT and macOS use hybrid designs — core services in kernel for speed, but with modular subsystems.
topics.real_world_analogy: Monolithic is like a single-room apartment where kitchen, bedroom, and bathroom are all in one space — fast to move around but messy. Layered is a multi-story building with strict floor access rules. Microkernel is a campus with separate buildings connected by roads (IPC) — one building burning down doesn't affect others. Hybrid is a modern office with an open floor plan but separate secured server rooms.
why_it_exists: Monolithic kernels provide maximum performance by avoiding user-kernel transitions for internal operations.
Microkernels provide maximum reliability — a buggy device driver crashes only its own user-space process, not the entire OS.
Hybrid kernels balance performance and modularity for practical real-world use cases.
tech_world: Linux is monolithic but uses Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) to dynamically load/unload device drivers without rebooting.
QNX (microkernel) is used in safety-critical systems like car infotainment and nuclear power plant controllers.
macOS uses XNU — a hybrid kernel combining Mach microkernel IPC with BSD monolithic subsystem.
key_points: Monolithic: All OS services in kernel space. Fast but one bug can crash the entire OS. Example: Linux, classic Unix.
Layered: Hierarchical layers with strict dependencies. Clean but slow due to layer traversal overhead.
Microkernel: Minimal kernel (IPC + scheduling). Drivers in user-space. Secure but slower. Example: QNX, L4, Mach.
Hybrid: Practical combination. Example: Windows NT (NT kernel), macOS (XNU = Mach + BSD).
Linux uses Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) for dynamic driver loading without rebooting.
interview_focus: Compare Monolithic vs Microkernel architecture with trade-offs.
Why is Linux considered monolithic even though it has loadable modules?

interview_questions.question: What is the difference between a Monolithic Kernel and a Microkernel?
interview_questions.answer:
**Monolithic Kernel**: All OS services (file system, device drivers, networking, memory management) run in kernel mode within a single large binary. Advantages: High performance (no user-kernel switching for internal calls), direct function calls between subsystems. Disadvantages: A bug in any driver can crash the entire OS; harder to maintain.

**Microkernel**: Only essential services (IPC, basic scheduling, memory mapping) run in kernel mode. File systems, drivers, and networking run as separate user-space server processes communicating via IPC. Advantages: High reliability (driver crash isolated to its process), easier to extend. Disadvantages: Slower due to frequent context switches and IPC overhead.

Examples: Linux = Monolithic; QNX, MINIX = Microkernel; Windows NT, macOS = Hybrid.

topics.title: Monolithic Kernel
topics.what_is_it: A kernel architecture where ALL OS services — process management, memory management, file systems, device drivers, and networking — run together in a single, large kernel-mode process sharing the same address space.
topics.simple_explanation:
In a monolithic kernel, the entire OS runs as one giant program in kernel mode:

- File system code can directly call memory management functions — no context switch needed.
- Device drivers run inside the kernel — they have direct access to hardware registers and kernel data structures.
- When you call `read()`, execution flows from your user-space program into the kernel's VFS layer → specific filesystem code (ext4) → block device driver → disk controller — all within the same kernel address space.

**Performance advantage**: Internal function calls between kernel subsystems are simple C function calls (nanoseconds). In a microkernel, the same interaction requires IPC message passing (microseconds).

**Reliability disadvantage**: A buggy NVIDIA driver running inside the Linux kernel can corrupt kernel memory and crash the entire system (kernel panic). In a microkernel, that driver would crash only its own user-space process.
topics.real_world_analogy: A monolithic kernel is like a restaurant where the chef, waiter, cashier, and dishwasher all work in one big open kitchen. Communication is instant (just shout across the room), but if the dishwasher accidentally starts a grease fire, the entire kitchen burns down — including your food.
why_it_exists: Function calls between subsystems are 100-1000x faster than IPC message passing used by microkernels.
Shared kernel address space enables zero-copy data transfer between subsystems.
Linux, the dominant server OS, chose monolithic architecture for maximum I/O and networking throughput.
tech_world: Linux kernel is monolithic — all 28+ million lines of code run in kernel mode, including 3000+ device drivers.
Kernel panics in Linux production servers are often caused by buggy third-party kernel modules (GPU drivers, filesystem modules).
Linux mitigates monolithic risks with Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) — drivers can be loaded/unloaded at runtime without rebooting.
key_points: All OS services share a single kernel address space — direct function calls, no IPC overhead.
Performance: Internal calls are nanosecond-level C function calls.
Risk: A single buggy driver can corrupt kernel memory → kernel panic → system crash.
Linux uses LKMs to add/remove drivers dynamically: `insmod`, `rmmod`, `modprobe`.
Examples: Linux, FreeBSD, classic Unix, Solaris.
interview_focus: Why did Linux choose monolithic architecture despite reliability risks?
How do Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) provide modularity within a monolithic kernel?

interview_questions.question: How does Linux achieve modularity despite being a monolithic kernel?
interview_questions.answer: Linux uses Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs). These are compiled `.ko` files that can be dynamically loaded into and unloaded from the running kernel without rebooting. Commands: `insmod` (insert module), `rmmod` (remove module), `modprobe` (load with dependency resolution). Device drivers, filesystem implementations, and network protocols are commonly distributed as LKMs. While they run in kernel space (monolithic), they can be added/removed on-the-fly, providing practical modularity.

topics.title: Microkernel
topics.what_is_it: A minimalist kernel architecture where only the most essential services (IPC message passing, basic CPU scheduling, and low-level memory mapping) run in kernel mode. All other services — file systems, device drivers, networking — run as isolated user-space server processes.
topics.simple_explanation:
A microkernel follows the philosophy of 'less code in kernel = fewer bugs that crash the system':

- **Kernel contains only**: IPC mechanism, thread/process scheduling, virtual memory mapping, and interrupt handling.
- **Everything else runs in user-space**: File system server, network server, device driver servers.
- **Communication**: When a process wants to read a file, it sends an IPC message to the file system server (user-space process). The FS server processes the request and sends a reply message back.

**Why it's safer**: If the WiFi driver crashes, only the WiFi driver process dies. The kernel, file system, and all other processes continue running unaffected. In a monolithic kernel, the same crash would cause a kernel panic.

**Why it's slower**: Every file read requires: User process → kernel IPC → FS server (user-space) → kernel IPC → block device driver (user-space) → kernel IPC → back to user process. That's 6+ context switches vs 0 in monolithic.
topics.real_world_analogy: A microkernel is like a corporate headquarters where only the CEO and receptionist (minimal kernel) work in the main building. All departments (HR, Finance, Engineering = file system, networking, drivers) work in separate buildings. Communication happens via formal memos (IPC messages). If the HR building catches fire, the CEO's building is unaffected.
why_it_exists: Safety-critical systems (medical devices, avionics, nuclear reactors) cannot tolerate OS crashes caused by driver bugs.
Formal verification becomes feasible when the kernel is only 10,000 lines instead of 28 million (seL4 microkernel is formally proven correct).
Hot-restarting a crashed user-space driver is trivial; recovering from a kernel panic requires full system reboot.
tech_world: QNX powers BlackBerry cars, BMW/Audi infotainment systems, and medical devices — industries where reliability is non-negotiable.
seL4 is a formally verified microkernel mathematically proven to be bug-free — used in military drones and autonomous vehicles.
MINIX (microkernel) runs inside Intel Management Engine on every modern Intel CPU — you're running a microkernel right now without knowing it.
key_points: Kernel only contains: IPC, scheduling, memory mapping — typically < 50,000 lines of code.
File systems, drivers, and networking run as isolated user-space server processes.
Reliability: Driver crash = only that service restarts. No kernel panic.
Performance: Slower than monolithic due to IPC message passing overhead and frequent context switches.
Examples: QNX, L4, seL4, MINIX, Mach (basis of macOS XNU kernel).
interview_focus: Why are microkernels preferred for safety-critical systems?
What is the performance cost of microkernel architecture?

interview_questions.question: Why are microkernels not widely used in general-purpose operating systems despite being more reliable?
interview_questions.answer: The primary reason is performance. Every interaction between OS services requires IPC message passing through the kernel, involving multiple context switches and data copies. A simple file read in a microkernel involves: user process → kernel → FS server → kernel → disk driver → kernel → user process (6+ context switches). In a monolithic kernel like Linux, the same operation is a direct function call chain within kernel space (0 extra context switches). For general-purpose workloads (web servers, databases), this performance overhead is unacceptable. However, for safety-critical domains (automotive, medical, aerospace), the reliability guarantee of isolated services outweighs the performance cost.

topics.title: Hybrid Kernel
topics.what_is_it: A pragmatic kernel architecture that combines the performance of monolithic kernels (running performance-critical services in kernel mode) with the modularity of microkernels (keeping some services as separate subsystems or user-space processes).
topics.simple_explanation:
Real-world operating systems don't follow pure monolithic or pure microkernel designs. They take the best of both worlds:

- **Windows NT Kernel**: Runs core services (I/O manager, memory manager, process manager) in kernel mode for performance. But uses a layered subsystem architecture where Win32, POSIX, and OS/2 subsystems run as separate user-mode processes.
- **macOS XNU**: Combines Mach microkernel (IPC and memory management) with FreeBSD monolithic kernel (file systems, networking, POSIX APIs) in a single kernel binary. Gets Mach's clean IPC design with BSD's performance.
- **Linux with LKMs**: Technically monolithic, but practically behaves like a hybrid — device drivers can be loaded/unloaded as modules, and technologies like FUSE allow file systems to run in user-space.
topics.real_world_analogy: A hybrid kernel is like a hospital. Critical departments (ER, Surgery, ICU) operate within the main building for speed (kernel mode). Non-critical services (cafeteria, gift shop, administrative offices) operate in separate buildings (user-space), connected by covered walkways.
why_it_exists: Pure monolithic is too risky for modern complex systems with thousands of drivers.
Pure microkernel is too slow for general-purpose computing workloads.
Hybrid balances performance and reliability for practical real-world operating systems.
tech_world: Windows 10/11 uses the NT hybrid kernel — HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer) in kernel, subsystems in user-mode.
macOS Ventura/Sonoma uses XNU = Mach (microkernel IPC) + BSD (monolithic file/network) + IOKit (driver framework).
ChromeOS runs a Linux kernel with heavy user-space isolation via sandboxing and namespaces — hybrid in practice.
key_points: Combines monolithic performance with microkernel modularity.
Performance-critical services (I/O, memory) in kernel space; less-critical services in user space.
Windows NT: Kernel mode executive + user-mode subsystems (Win32, POSIX).
macOS XNU: Mach microkernel IPC + BSD monolithic subsystem in one kernel binary.
Most modern OS are hybrid — pure designs are academic concepts.
interview_focus: Is Windows monolithic or microkernel? Explain its actual architecture.
What is macOS XNU kernel and how does it combine Mach with BSD?

interview_questions.question: Is the macOS kernel monolithic or microkernel?
interview_questions.answer:
Neither — it's a hybrid called XNU (X is Not Unix). XNU combines:
1. **Mach microkernel**: Provides IPC (Mach ports), virtual memory management, and task/thread abstractions.
2. **BSD layer**: Provides POSIX APIs, file systems (APFS, HFS+), networking stack (TCP/IP), and process model.
3. **IOKit**: Object-oriented C++ framework for device drivers.

Mach and BSD run together in a single kernel address space (like monolithic) for performance, but the internal architecture uses Mach's clean IPC abstractions. So XNU gets monolithic performance with microkernel design principles.

sections.description: Understand system calls, user vs kernel mode transitions, interrupts, traps, and the complete boot sequence from BIOS to userland.

topics.title: System Calls
topics.what_is_it: System calls (syscalls) are the programmatic interface through which user-space applications request privileged services from the OS kernel. They are the ONLY legal mechanism for user programs to access hardware, files, network, and other protected resources.
topics.simple_explanation:
Your application runs in 'user mode' where it CANNOT directly access hardware, other processes' memory, or kernel data structures. When it needs something privileged, it makes a **system call** — a controlled entry point into the kernel.

What happens during a syscall:
1. Application calls a wrapper function like `open('file.txt')` in C.
2. The C library (glibc) places the syscall number in a CPU register (e.g., `rax = 2` for `open` on x86-64).
3. A special CPU instruction is executed: `syscall` (x86-64) or `int 0x80` (legacy x86).
4. CPU switches from **User Mode (Ring 3)** to **Kernel Mode (Ring 0)**.
5. The kernel's syscall handler reads the syscall number, looks up the corresponding kernel function in the syscall table, and executes it.
6. Kernel performs the operation (opens the file, returns a file descriptor).
7. CPU switches back to User Mode, and control returns to the application.

Common syscalls: `open()`, `read()`, `write()`, `close()`, `fork()`, `exec()`, `mmap()`, `brk()`, `socket()`, `connect()`.
topics.real_world_analogy: A system call is like a bank withdrawal. You (user program) cannot walk into the vault (hardware) and grab cash. You fill out a withdrawal slip (syscall parameters), hand it to the teller (syscall handler) through a secured window (mode switch), the teller retrieves the cash from the vault (kernel operation), and hands it back to you through the window.
why_it_exists: Security: Without syscalls, any program could directly read/write disk sectors, accessing other users' files or corrupting the OS.
Stability: User programs cannot accidentally modify kernel data structures that would crash the entire system.
Abstraction: Applications call `write(fd, buf, size)` without knowing whether fd points to a terminal, file, pipe, or network socket.
tech_world: Linux kernel has ~450 system calls. You can list them with `ausyscall --dump`.
Strace traces every syscall a process makes: `strace -c node server.js` shows syscall frequency and latency.
High-performance servers minimize syscalls using techniques like `io_uring` (Linux 5.1+) which batches multiple I/O operations into a single syscall.
key_points: Syscalls are the ONLY legal way for user programs to request kernel services.
Mode switch: CPU transitions from Ring 3 (User) to Ring 0 (Kernel) during syscall.
Syscall overhead: ~100-200 nanoseconds per syscall due to mode switch, TLB flush, and register save/restore.
Common syscalls: open, read, write, close, fork, exec, mmap, socket, connect, ioctl.
Linux x86-64 uses the `syscall` instruction; syscall number passed in `rax` register.
interview_focus: What exactly happens when a system call is made? Describe the complete flow.
Why can't user programs directly access hardware?

interview_questions.question: Explain the complete flow of a system call from user space to kernel space and back.
interview_questions.answer:
Step-by-step flow:
1. **Library Call**: Application calls `read(fd, buf, n)` which invokes the C library (glibc) wrapper.
2. **Register Setup**: glibc places syscall number in `rax` (e.g., `rax = 0` for read on x86-64), and arguments in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx` registers.
3. **Trap Instruction**: `syscall` instruction triggers a CPU exception, switching from Ring 3 (User Mode) to Ring 0 (Kernel Mode).
4. **Save Context**: CPU saves user-space registers (instruction pointer, stack pointer, flags) onto the kernel stack.
5. **Syscall Dispatch**: Kernel reads `rax`, looks up `sys_read()` in the syscall table (`sys_call_table[0]`).
6. **Kernel Execution**: `sys_read()` validates the fd, checks permissions, reads data from the file's page cache or triggers disk I/O.
7. **Return**: Result placed in `rax`. CPU restores user-space registers, switches back to Ring 3.
8. **glibc Return**: If `rax` is negative, glibc sets `errno` and returns -1. Otherwise, returns the byte count.

topics.title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode
topics.what_is_it: Two distinct CPU execution privilege levels: User Mode (Ring 3) where applications run with restricted access, and Kernel Mode (Ring 0) where the OS kernel runs with full hardware access. The CPU hardware enforces this separation.
topics.simple_explanation:
Modern CPUs have hardware-enforced privilege rings (x86 has Ring 0 through Ring 3):

**User Mode (Ring 3):**
- Where your applications, browsers, editors run.
- CANNOT execute privileged CPU instructions (`hlt`, `cli`, `in`/`out` for I/O ports).
- CANNOT access physical memory directly — only virtual addresses mapped by the kernel.
- CANNOT access other processes' memory.
- If it tries anything forbidden → CPU raises a Protection Fault → OS kills the process (SIGSEGV).

**Kernel Mode (Ring 0):**
- Where the OS kernel runs.
- CAN execute ALL CPU instructions including privileged ones.
- CAN access ALL physical memory, hardware registers, and I/O ports.
- CAN modify page tables, interrupt vectors, and CPU control registers.
- A bug here can corrupt the entire system — kernel panic.

The transition between modes happens via: system calls (user→kernel), interrupts (hardware→kernel), and return instructions (kernel→user).
topics.real_world_analogy: User Mode is the passenger cabin of an airplane. You can use the entertainment system, call the flight attendant, and use the restroom. Kernel Mode is the cockpit — only trained pilots (the kernel) can access flight controls. If a passenger tries to enter the cockpit (privileged instruction in user mode), air marshals (CPU protection) intervene.
why_it_exists: Without dual-mode operation, any program could halt the CPU (`hlt`), disable interrupts (`cli`), or overwrite kernel memory.
Hardware-enforced protection means even intentionally malicious code cannot bypass the privilege boundary.
OS stability depends on preventing application code from corrupting kernel data structures.
tech_world: The `/proc/[pid]/status` file shows whether a process is running in user or kernel mode via `voluntary_ctxt_switches` and `nonvoluntary_ctxt_switches`.
The `top` command shows `%us` (user mode CPU%) vs `%sy` (kernel/system mode CPU%). High `%sy` means excessive system calls or kernel activity.
Spectre/Meltdown CPU vulnerabilities exploited weaknesses in the user-kernel boundary, allowing user-mode code to read kernel memory.
key_points: User Mode (Ring 3): Restricted CPU instructions, virtual memory only, no hardware access.
Kernel Mode (Ring 0): Full CPU access, physical memory access, hardware register control.
Mode Switch Trigger: System calls, hardware interrupts, exceptions/traps.
Mode Bit: A single bit in the CPU status register indicates current privilege level.
Attempting privileged instructions in User Mode → CPU Protection Fault → OS sends SIGSEGV.
interview_focus: What is the difference between User Mode and Kernel Mode?
What happens when a user-mode program tries to execute a privileged instruction?

interview_questions.question: What is the difference between User Mode and Kernel Mode? Why is this separation necessary?
interview_questions.answer:
**User Mode (Ring 3)**: Application code runs with restricted privileges. Cannot access hardware directly, execute privileged CPU instructions, or touch other processes' memory. If it attempts forbidden operations, the CPU raises a hardware exception.

**Kernel Mode (Ring 0)**: OS kernel runs with full hardware access. Can execute any CPU instruction, access any memory address, and control all devices.

**Why necessary**: Without this separation, any application could: (1) Read other processes' passwords from memory, (2) Overwrite OS kernel code, (3) Halt the CPU with `hlt` instruction, (4) Disable all interrupts with `cli`, permanently freezing the system. The CPU hardware enforces this boundary — it's not just a software convention.

topics.title: Interrupts & Interrupt Handling
topics.what_is_it: An interrupt is a hardware or software signal that causes the CPU to immediately pause current execution, save its state, and jump to a pre-defined Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) in the kernel to handle the event.
topics.simple_explanation:
Interrupts are how hardware devices communicate urgently with the CPU:

**Hardware Interrupts (Asynchronous):**
- Keyboard pressed → keyboard controller sends interrupt to CPU.
- Network packet arrives → NIC sends interrupt.
- Disk read complete → disk controller sends interrupt.
- Timer tick → hardware timer sends interrupt every 1-10ms (drives scheduling).

**Software Interrupts/Traps (Synchronous):**
- System call → `syscall` instruction (intentional trap).
- Division by zero → CPU exception.
- Page fault → MMU detects unmapped page.

**Interrupt Handling Flow:**
1. Device sends interrupt signal to CPU via Interrupt Request Line (IRQ).
2. CPU finishes current instruction, saves registers and Program Counter on stack.
3. CPU reads Interrupt Descriptor Table (IDT) to find the ISR address for this interrupt number.
4. CPU switches to Kernel Mode and jumps to the ISR.
5. ISR handles the event (reads keyboard key, processes network packet).
6. ISR sends End-of-Interrupt (EOI) signal to interrupt controller.
7. CPU restores saved registers and resumes the interrupted process.
topics.real_world_analogy: Interrupts are like a doorbell. You're working at your desk (CPU executing a process). The doorbell rings (interrupt signal). You pause your work, save your place (save registers), go answer the door (run ISR), handle the visitor (process the event), and return to your desk to resume work exactly where you left off.
why_it_exists: Without interrupts, the CPU would need to constantly poll every device ('is a key pressed? is a packet ready?') — wasting enormous CPU cycles.
Interrupts enable asynchronous event-driven I/O: CPU does useful work until a device signals completion.
Timer interrupts are essential for preemptive multitasking — without them, a process running an infinite loop would permanently hold the CPU.
tech_world: In Linux, `/proc/interrupts` shows real-time interrupt counts per CPU core per IRQ line.
Network-intensive servers can see millions of interrupts/second from NIC — Linux NAPI (interrupt coalescing) batches packets to reduce interrupt overhead.
The timer interrupt frequency (HZ) in Linux kernel is typically 250Hz or 1000Hz — configurable at compile time.
key_points: Hardware interrupts: Asynchronous signals from devices (keyboard, NIC, disk, timer).
Software interrupts (Traps): Synchronous signals from CPU exceptions (page fault, division by zero, syscall).
IDT (Interrupt Descriptor Table): Maps interrupt numbers to ISR handler addresses.
ISR must be fast — complex work is deferred to 'bottom half' handlers (softirqs, tasklets, work queues).
Timer interrupt drives preemptive scheduling: every 1-10ms, scheduler gets a chance to switch processes.
interview_focus: What is the difference between hardware interrupts and software traps?
Why are timer interrupts critical for preemptive multitasking?

interview_questions.question: What is the difference between an interrupt and a trap?
interview_questions.answer:
**Interrupt (Hardware)**: Asynchronous signal generated by external hardware devices (keyboard, NIC, disk controller, timer). The CPU can be interrupted at any point during execution. The CPU finishes the current instruction, saves state, and jumps to the ISR.

**Trap (Software)**: Synchronous signal generated by the CPU itself during instruction execution. Causes: (1) Intentional traps — system calls (`syscall` instruction). (2) Unintentional exceptions — division by zero, page faults, illegal instruction, segmentation fault.

Key difference: Interrupts come from OUTSIDE the CPU (hardware); Traps originate INSIDE the CPU (during instruction execution).

topics.title: Boot Process (Power-On to User Space)
topics.what_is_it: The complete sequence from pressing the power button to reaching the login screen: BIOS/UEFI firmware initialization → bootloader (GRUB) → kernel loading → init system (systemd) → user-space services.
topics.simple_explanation:
When you press the power button, the following chain executes:

1. **BIOS/UEFI (Firmware)**: CPU starts executing firmware code stored in ROM chip on motherboard. Performs POST (Power-On Self Test) — checks CPU, RAM, GPU, disks are functional. Identifies bootable device (SSD/USB/Network).
2. **Bootloader (GRUB/Windows Boot Manager)**: Firmware loads the bootloader from the boot sector (MBR) or EFI System Partition. GRUB displays the OS selection menu and loads the Linux kernel binary (`vmlinuz`) and initial ramdisk (`initramfs`) into memory.
3. **Kernel Initialization**: Kernel decompresses itself, initializes CPU, memory management (page tables), interrupt handlers, and device drivers. Mounts the root filesystem.
4. **Init Process (PID 1)**: Kernel starts the first user-space process — `systemd` (modern Linux) or `init` (legacy). PID 1 is the ancestor of ALL user-space processes.
5. **systemd Services**: systemd reads unit files and starts services in parallel: networking, logging (journald), SSH server, Docker daemon, display manager (GDM/SDDM for GUI login).
6. **Login**: Display manager shows login screen, or TTY shows shell prompt.
topics.real_world_analogy: Booting is like opening a restaurant. BIOS = checking if gas, electricity, and water work (POST). Bootloader = finding the recipe book (loading the kernel). Kernel init = turning on ovens, grills, and fridges (hardware drivers). systemd = hiring waiters, chefs, and dishwashers (starting services). Login = opening the front door to customers.
why_it_exists: CPU starts in a minimal state with no OS loaded — firmware bootstraps the system enough to load the actual OS.
GRUB allows choosing between multiple installed OS (dual boot Linux + Windows).
systemd parallelizes service startup, reducing boot time from minutes to seconds on modern systems.
tech_world: UEFI Secure Boot verifies kernel signatures to prevent rootkit-modified kernels from loading.
systemd tracks service dependencies as a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) and starts independent services in parallel.
`systemd-analyze blame` shows exactly which services slowed down your boot time.
`dmesg` shows kernel boot messages — invaluable for debugging hardware detection failures.
key_points: BIOS/UEFI: Firmware POST → find boot device → load bootloader.
GRUB: Load kernel (vmlinuz) + initramfs into RAM → transfer control to kernel.
Kernel: Hardware init → mount root FS → start PID 1 (systemd/init).
systemd: Parallel service startup via unit files → reach default target (multi-user or graphical).
PID 1 is special: if PID 1 dies, the kernel panics — the entire system crashes.
interview_focus: Walk through the boot process from power-on to login screen.
What is PID 1 and why is it special?

interview_questions.question: What happens from the moment you press the power button to seeing the Linux login prompt?
interview_questions.answer:
1. **CPU resets** and starts executing firmware (BIOS/UEFI) at a fixed address (0xFFFFFFF0 on x86).
2. **POST**: Firmware tests CPU, RAM, and peripheral hardware.
3. **Boot device selection**: Firmware reads boot order and locates the bootable device.
4. **Bootloader (GRUB)**: Loaded from MBR/GPT. Displays OS menu, loads `vmlinuz` (compressed kernel) and `initramfs` into memory.
5. **Kernel decompression**: Kernel unpacks itself, sets up early memory management, and initializes GDT/IDT.
6. **Hardware initialization**: Kernel probes hardware, loads device drivers, and mounts root filesystem (from initramfs initially, then pivots to real root).
7. **PID 1 (systemd)**: Kernel executes `/sbin/init` → systemd reads unit files → starts services (networking, SSH, logging) in parallel.
8. **Login manager**: `getty` spawns on TTYs for CLI login, or display manager (GDM) starts for GUI login.

sections.title: 03 Process Management & Lifecycle
sections.description: Understand process creation, states, PCB, context switching, fork/exec, and orphan/zombie processes.

topics.title: Process
topics.what_is_it: A process is a program in execution — an active entity with its own virtual address space, CPU registers, program counter, open file descriptors, and OS-managed resources. A program on disk is static code; a process is that code loaded into memory and actively running.
topics.simple_explanation:
A **program** is a passive file sitting on disk (`/usr/bin/node`). A **process** is that program loaded into memory and executing.

Every process has its own isolated resources:
- **Virtual Address Space**: Code segment (instructions), data segment (globals), heap (dynamic allocation via `malloc`/`new`), and stack (local variables, function call frames).
- **Program Counter (PC)**: Points to the next instruction to execute.
- **CPU Registers**: Current computation state.
- **Open File Descriptors**: stdin (0), stdout (1), stderr (2), plus any opened files/sockets.
- **Process ID (PID)**: Unique integer identifier assigned by the OS.
- **Process Control Block (PCB)**: Kernel data structure (`task_struct` in Linux) storing all process metadata.

One program can have multiple processes: opening 3 Chrome windows creates 3 separate processes of the same Chrome binary.
topics.real_world_analogy: A program is like a recipe book sitting on a shelf. A process is a chef actively cooking a dish following that recipe. The chef has their own cutting board (memory), position in the recipe (program counter), ingredients on the counter (registers), and a workstation number (PID). Multiple chefs can cook the same recipe simultaneously — each is a separate process.
why_it_exists: Processes provide isolation: one crashing process cannot corrupt another's memory.
Processes enable multitasking: 100 processes can share 4 CPU cores via scheduling.
Processes provide security boundaries: each process runs with a specific user identity and permissions.
tech_world: Chrome uses multi-process architecture: each tab runs in a separate sandboxed process. If one tab crashes (SIGSEGV), other tabs continue running.
`ps aux` lists all running processes with PID, CPU%, memory%, and command.
Linux's `task_struct` (PCB) is approximately 10KB per process — containing ~200 fields tracking every aspect of process state.
key_points: Program = passive file on disk. Process = active program in execution with its own resources.
Each process has: virtual address space (code + data + heap + stack), PID, registers, program counter, open file descriptors.
PCB (task_struct in Linux): Kernel data structure storing ALL process metadata.
One program → multiple processes (e.g., 3 Chrome windows = 3 processes).
Process isolation: separate virtual address spaces prevent one process from accessing another's memory.
interview_focus: What is the difference between a process and a program?
What information does the PCB (Process Control Block) contain?

interview_questions.question: What is the difference between a Program and a Process?
interview_questions.answer:
**Program**: A static, passive entity — a file containing compiled machine code stored on disk (e.g., `/usr/bin/python3`). It has no state and consumes no CPU or memory resources.

**Process**: An active, dynamic entity — a program loaded into memory and currently executing. It has: (1) Its own virtual address space (code, data, heap, stack), (2) CPU state (registers, program counter), (3) OS resources (PID, open file descriptors, security credentials), (4) Execution state (running, waiting, ready).

Analogy: A program is a recipe written on paper. A process is the act of cooking that recipe — with ingredients on the counter, timers running, and pots on the stove.

topics.title: Process States & Transitions
topics.what_is_it: Processes transition through 5 defined states during their lifecycle: New → Ready → Running → Waiting (Blocked) → Terminated. The OS scheduler manages these transitions.
topics.simple_explanation:
A process moves through these states:

1. **New**: Process is being created. Binary being loaded, PCB being allocated, memory being set up.
2. **Ready**: Process is loaded in memory and WAITING for CPU time. It's sitting in the Ready Queue. Multiple processes compete for limited CPU cores.
3. **Running**: Process is actively executing on a CPU core. Only 1 process per core can be Running at any instant.
4. **Waiting (Blocked)**: Process is waiting for an I/O event (disk read, network response, user input). It CANNOT run even if CPU is free. Once I/O completes, it moves back to Ready.
5. **Terminated (Zombie)**: Process finished execution. Its exit code is stored, but the PCB still exists until the parent calls `wait()` to collect the exit status.

**Key Transitions:**
- Ready → Running: Scheduler picks this process to run (CPU dispatch).
- Running → Ready: Timer interrupt fires; scheduler preempts the process (time slice expired).
- Running → Waiting: Process calls blocking I/O (e.g., `read()` on disk).
- Waiting → Ready: I/O operation completes; process re-enters the ready queue.
- Running → Terminated: Process calls `exit()` or receives a fatal signal (SIGKILL).
topics.real_world_analogy: Process states are like a patient's journey in a hospital. New = Admission paperwork. Ready = Sitting in the waiting room. Running = Doctor is examining you. Waiting = Sent to X-ray lab (waiting for results). Terminated = Discharged. A patient kicked out of the doctor's office because their time is up goes back to the waiting room (Running → Ready preemption).
why_it_exists: The scheduler needs to know which processes are ready to run to make CPU allocation decisions.
Separating Waiting from Ready prevents the scheduler from assigning CPU to a process that's blocked on I/O.
The Zombie state ensures the parent process can retrieve exit codes for error handling.
tech_world: `ps aux` shows process states: R (Running/Runnable), S (Sleeping/Waiting), D (Uninterruptible Sleep — waiting for disk I/O), Z (Zombie), T (Stopped).
A process in D state (Uninterruptible Sleep) cannot be killed even with `kill -9` — it's waiting for hardware I/O completion.
High number of processes in D state indicates I/O bottleneck (slow disk, NFS mount issues).
key_points: 5 states: New → Ready → Running → Waiting → Terminated.
Only 1 process per CPU core can be in Running state at any instant.
Ready → Running: Scheduler dispatches the process to a CPU core.
Running → Ready: Preemption by timer interrupt (time quantum expired).
Running → Waiting: Process issues blocking I/O syscall.
Waiting → Ready: I/O completion interrupt wakes the process.
Zombie (Z): Terminated but PCB retained until parent calls wait().
interview_focus: Draw and explain the 5-state process lifecycle diagram.
What is the difference between Ready and Waiting states?

interview_questions.question: Can a process go directly from Waiting state to Running state?
interview_questions.answer: No. When a process's I/O completes, it transitions from Waiting → Ready (placed back in the ready queue). It must then wait for the scheduler to select it before it transitions from Ready → Running. Even if the CPU is idle, the scheduler dispatches from the ready queue — maintaining the standard state transition model. The only exception is some real-time schedulers that can immediately dispatch a newly-ready high-priority process.

topics.title: PCB (Process Control Block)
topics.what_is_it: The PCB (Process Control Block) is the kernel data structure that stores ALL metadata about a process. In Linux, this structure is called `task_struct` (~10KB per process). Every process has exactly one PCB, and the OS uses it to manage, schedule, and context-switch processes.
topics.simple_explanation:
When the OS creates a process, it allocates a `task_struct` containing:

- **Process ID (PID)** and Parent PID (PPID)
- **Process State**: Running, Ready, Waiting, Zombie, etc.
- **CPU Registers**: Saved register values (restored during context switch)
- **Program Counter**: Address of the next instruction to execute
- **Memory Management Info**: Pointer to the process's page table (virtual → physical address mapping)
- **Scheduling Info**: Priority, nice value, time quantum remaining, scheduling policy (SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR)
- **I/O Status**: List of open file descriptors and their positions
- **Accounting Info**: Total CPU time consumed, creation timestamp, user/group ID
- **Signal Handlers**: Table of registered signal handlers (SIGINT → custom handler)

During a context switch, the OS saves the current process's CPU registers into its PCB, then loads the next process's registers from its PCB — this is how the illusion of parallelism works on a single CPU core.
topics.real_world_analogy: A PCB is like a student's academic file maintained by the university registrar. It contains: student ID (PID), enrollment status (process state), current grades (CPU registers), next class to attend (program counter), hostel room assignment (memory info), scholarship details (priority), and library card number (file descriptors). When a student goes on leave, the file is stored; when they return, their details are loaded back.
why_it_exists: Context switching requires saving and restoring exact CPU state — the PCB is where this state is stored.
The scheduler reads PCB fields (priority, state, time consumed) to make scheduling decisions.
The memory manager uses PCB's page table pointer to translate virtual addresses for the correct process.
tech_world: Linux's `task_struct` is defined in `include/linux/sched.h` — it's approximately 10KB with ~200 fields.
`/proc/[pid]/status` exposes PCB fields: State, PPid, Threads, VmSize, VmRSS, voluntary_ctxt_switches.
Each `task_struct` is stored in a doubly-linked list and a red-black tree for O(log n) scheduler lookup.
key_points: PCB = task_struct in Linux, approximately 10KB per process.
Contains: PID, state, registers, PC, page table pointer, file descriptors, scheduling priority, signals.
Context switch = save current PCB → load next PCB → resume execution.
Stored in kernel memory — user processes cannot directly access their own PCB.
Scheduler maintains a queue of PCBs organized by state (ready queue, wait queue).
interview_focus: What information does a PCB contain?
How is the PCB used during a context switch?

interview_questions.question: What is a Process Control Block and what does it contain?
interview_questions.answer:
A PCB is the kernel data structure (called `task_struct` in Linux) that stores all metadata about a process. It contains:
1. **Identification**: PID, PPID, User ID, Group ID.
2. **CPU State**: Saved register values, Program Counter, Stack Pointer, CPU flags.
3. **Scheduling**: Process state (ready/running/waiting), priority, nice value, scheduling policy, CPU time consumed.
4. **Memory**: Pointer to process's page table, virtual memory area (VMA) list, memory limits.
5. **I/O**: Array of open file descriptors, current working directory, root directory.
6. **Signals**: Pending signals mask, registered signal handlers.
7. **Accounting**: Start time, total user/kernel CPU time.

The PCB is critical for context switching — the OS saves the running process's registers into its PCB and loads the next process's registers from its PCB.

topics.title: Context Switching
topics.what_is_it: A context switch is the mechanism by which the OS saves the complete CPU state (registers, program counter, stack pointer) of the currently running process into its PCB and loads the saved CPU state of the next process from its PCB — allowing the CPU to resume executing the new process exactly where it left off.
topics.simple_explanation:
Since a 4-core CPU can only run 4 processes simultaneously, the OS rapidly switches between processes to create the illusion of running 200 processes at once. This switching is called a **context switch**.

**What happens during a context switch:**
1. Timer interrupt fires (e.g., every 4ms = time quantum).
2. CPU switches to kernel mode.
3. Kernel saves Process A's registers (RAX, RBX, ..., RIP, RSP, RFLAGS) into Process A's PCB.
4. Kernel runs the scheduler algorithm to pick the next process (Process B).
5. Kernel loads Process B's saved registers from Process B's PCB into the CPU.
6. Kernel updates the Memory Management Unit (MMU) to point to Process B's page table — this flushes the TLB.
7. CPU switches back to user mode and resumes executing Process B.

**Cost of context switch:**
- Direct cost: ~1-10 microseconds for register save/restore + page table switch.
- Indirect cost: TLB flush means the new process starts with cache misses (cold cache) — can cause 100s of microseconds of performance loss.
- Total effective cost: 5-50 microseconds depending on working set size.
topics.real_world_analogy: A context switch is like a judge switching between cases in a courtroom. Before moving to the next case, the judge saves all notes, evidence documents, and the current state of arguments for Case A (save PCB). Then loads all documents for Case B (load PCB). The mental cost of re-reading and understanding the new case context is the 'cache warmup' overhead.
why_it_exists: Enables preemptive multitasking — the OS forcibly switches away from a running process after its time quantum expires.
Without context switching, a single process running an infinite loop would permanently monopolize the CPU.
Allows the CPU to do useful work while one process is blocked waiting for I/O.
tech_world: Linux context switch takes approximately 2-5 microseconds on modern hardware.
`vmstat 1` shows context switches per second in the `cs` column. A web server might see 50,000-200,000 cs/sec.
Excessive context switching (>100K/sec) indicates too many runnable processes competing for limited CPU cores — consider scaling horizontally.
Thread context switches are cheaper than process context switches because threads share the same page table (no TLB flush needed).
key_points: Context switch = save current process state + load next process state + switch page tables.
Triggered by: timer interrupt (preemption), I/O blocking, yield(), higher-priority process arriving.
Direct cost: ~1-10 microseconds (register save/restore + page table update).
Indirect cost: TLB flush + cache pollution → cold cache misses (major performance impact).
Thread switches are cheaper than process switches — threads share page tables, so no TLB flush.
interview_focus: What happens during a context switch? List the steps.
Why are context switches expensive? What is the hidden cost?

interview_questions.question: Why is a context switch between threads cheaper than between processes?
interview_questions.answer:
When switching between two threads of the SAME process:
- They share the same virtual address space → NO page table switch needed → NO TLB flush.
- They share the same code, data, and heap segments.
- Only thread-specific state needs saving: CPU registers, program counter, and stack pointer.

When switching between two different processes:
- Each has its own virtual address space → page table must be switched (update CR3 register on x86).
- TLB is flushed (or tagged entries invalidated) → subsequent memory accesses suffer cache misses.
- The indirect cost of TLB misses can be 10-50x more expensive than the register save/restore alone.

This is why multi-threaded servers (Nginx worker threads) prefer threads over processes for concurrent request handling.

topics.title: fork() and exec() System Calls
topics.what_is_it: fork() creates a new child process by duplicating the calling (parent) process. exec() replaces the current process's memory with a new program binary. Together, fork() + exec() is the standard Unix mechanism for running new programs.
topics.simple_explanation:
**fork():**
- Creates an almost identical copy of the parent process.
- Child gets a NEW PID but inherits: open file descriptors, memory contents, environment variables, signal handlers.
- Returns twice: returns child's PID to parent, returns 0 to child.
- Memory is NOT immediately copied — Linux uses **Copy-on-Write (COW)**: parent and child share the same physical pages until one of them writes, at which point only the modified page is copied.

**exec() family (execve, execvp, execlp):**
- Replaces the current process's code, data, heap, and stack with a new program binary.
- PID stays the same — it's the SAME process running a different program.
- Open file descriptors are preserved (unless marked close-on-exec).
- There is no return from exec() on success — the old code no longer exists.

**Fork + Exec pattern (how `bash` runs commands):**
```
bash (PID 100) calls fork()
  → child (PID 101) is a copy of bash
  → child calls exec("/usr/bin/ls")
  → child's memory is replaced with `ls` binary
  → child runs ls, prints files, exits
  → parent (bash) calls wait() to collect child's exit status
```
topics.real_world_analogy: fork() is like a cell dividing — you get two nearly identical cells (processes). exec() is like one of those cells undergoing complete metamorphosis into a butterfly (replacing its entire program). Shell commands are: fork (create clone) → exec (transform clone into the new program) → wait (parent waits for the child to finish).
why_it_exists: Fork provides a simple mechanism to create new processes — the child automatically inherits the parent's environment.
Exec separates process creation from program execution — allowing setup between fork and exec (redirect I/O, change directory, drop privileges).
Copy-on-Write makes fork() extremely fast — no actual memory copying occurs until pages are modified.
tech_world: Nginx master process forks worker processes at startup. Workers inherit the listening socket from the master.
Redis uses fork() for background BGSAVE — the child writes the RDB snapshot while the parent continues serving requests (COW ensures minimal memory overhead).
Node.js `child_process.fork()` creates a new Node.js process with a built-in IPC channel to the parent.
key_points: fork() duplicates the process: same code, data, file descriptors. Child gets PID > 0 from fork; parent gets child PID; child gets 0.
Copy-on-Write (COW): Physical memory shared until either process writes → only modified pages are copied.
exec() replaces entire process memory with new binary. PID unchanged. No return on success.
Fork + Exec + Wait: Standard Unix pattern for running programs.
Orphan: Parent dies before child → child adopted by PID 1 (init/systemd).
Zombie: Child exits but parent hasn't called wait() → PCB persists consuming PID slot.
interview_focus: What is fork()? What does it return and to whom?
What is the fork + exec + wait pattern?
What is Copy-on-Write and why does it make fork() efficient?

interview_questions.question: What is a Zombie process and how do you fix it?
interview_questions.answer:
A **Zombie process** is a process that has completed execution (called `exit()`) but its entry in the process table (PCB/task_struct) is NOT removed because the parent process hasn't called `wait()` or `waitpid()` to read the child's exit status.

**Why it exists**: Unix design requires the parent to retrieve the child's exit code — so the kernel keeps the PCB alive until the parent collects it.

**Problem**: Zombies consume a PID slot and a small amount of kernel memory. Too many zombies can exhaust the PID space (default max 32768 on Linux), preventing new process creation.

**Fix**: (1) Fix the parent code to call `wait()` or install `SIGCHLD` handler with `SA_NOCLDWAIT`. (2) Kill the parent process — orphaned zombies are adopted by init/systemd (PID 1), which automatically calls `wait()` to reap them. (3) Use `signal(SIGCHLD, SIG_IGN)` to tell the kernel to auto-reap children.

**Detection**: `ps aux | grep Z` — zombie processes show state 'Z' (defunct).

topics.title: Orphan & Zombie Processes
topics.what_is_it: An Orphan process is a child process whose parent has terminated. A Zombie process is a child process that has terminated but whose parent hasn't yet called wait() to collect its exit status — the PCB lingers in the process table.
topics.simple_explanation:
**Orphan Process:**
- Parent process dies/exits before the child finishes.
- The orphaned child is automatically adopted by PID 1 (init/systemd).
- PID 1 will eventually call `wait()` on the orphan when it terminates.
- Orphans are NOT harmful — they run normally under their new parent (PID 1).

**Zombie Process:**
- Child process calls `exit()` and terminates.
- Kernel releases all child's resources (memory, file descriptors) EXCEPT the PCB entry in the process table.
- PCB is kept because it stores the child's exit code, which the parent might want to read via `wait()`.
- If the parent NEVER calls `wait()`, the zombie PCB persists forever.
- Zombies consume a PID number and ~64 bytes of kernel memory per zombie.
- You CANNOT kill a zombie with `kill -9` — it's already dead. You must either fix the parent or kill the parent.

**Zombie flood danger**: Linux default PID limit is 32768. If a buggy server forks children without calling `wait()`, it can accumulate thousands of zombies and exhaust the PID space → no new processes can be created → system effectively hangs.
topics.real_world_analogy: An orphan is a child whose parents died — the government (PID 1) takes responsibility. A zombie is like a death certificate that nobody collected from the hospital. The body (process resources) is cremated (freed), but the paperwork (PCB with exit code) sits in a filing cabinet taking up space until the family (parent process) comes to collect it.
why_it_exists: Zombie state ensures the parent can retrieve the child's exit status — important for error handling in shell scripts (`$?` variable).
Orphan adoption by PID 1 prevents permanently parentless processes that nobody can manage or reap.
Unix process hierarchy model requires every process to have exactly one parent.
tech_world: Docker containers that don't handle SIGCHLD properly accumulate zombies — this is why `tini` or `dumb-init` is used as PID 1 in containers.
`ps aux | awk '$8 == "Z" {print}'` — list all zombie processes.
Production Node.js servers using `child_process.fork()` must listen for the `exit` event to reap children.
key_points: Orphan: Parent dies first → child adopted by PID 1. Harmless, runs normally.
Zombie: Child dies but parent didn't call wait(). PCB persists. Cannot be killed (already dead).
Fix zombie: (1) Fix parent to call wait(), (2) Kill the parent (orphans then reaped by PID 1), (3) signal(SIGCHLD, SIG_IGN).
Zombie consumes: 1 PID slot + ~64 bytes kernel memory. No CPU, no user memory.
Docker PID 1 problem: If your app is PID 1 in a container and doesn't reap children → zombie accumulation.
interview_focus: What is the difference between an orphan process and a zombie process?
How do you prevent and remove zombie processes?

interview_questions.question: What is the difference between an Orphan process and a Zombie process?
interview_questions.answer:
**Orphan Process**: A running child whose parent has already terminated. The OS automatically re-parents it to PID 1 (init/systemd). The orphan continues running normally — it is NOT harmful.

**Zombie Process**: A terminated child whose parent has NOT called `wait()` to read its exit status. The process is dead (resources freed), but its PCB entry persists in the process table. You cannot kill it with `kill -9` because it's already dead.

**Key differences**: Orphan is alive but parentless. Zombie is dead but uncollected. Orphan is harmless. Zombie wastes PID slots and can cause PID exhaustion if accumulated.

**Fix zombies**: Kill the parent process → zombies become orphans → PID 1 reaps them. Or fix the parent code to handle SIGCHLD / call wait().

sections.title: 04 Threads & Multithreading
sections.description: Understand threads, user vs kernel threads, multithreading models, and the benefits of multi-threaded programming.

topics.title: Threads
topics.what_is_it: A thread is the smallest unit of CPU execution within a process. Multiple threads within the same process share the code, data, and heap segments but each has its own stack, program counter, and register set. Threads enable concurrent execution within a single process.
topics.simple_explanation:
A process is a heavy-weight container. Creating a new process via `fork()` duplicates the entire address space. But what if you just need concurrent execution within the same program?

**Threads** are lightweight execution units INSIDE a process:
- **Shared between threads**: Code segment, data segment (globals), heap, open file descriptors, signal handlers, PID.
- **Private per thread**: Stack (local variables), program counter (where each thread is executing), registers, Thread ID (TID).

**Why threads over processes?**
1. **Creation speed**: Creating a thread is 10-100x faster than forking a process (no address space duplication).
2. **Memory efficiency**: 10 threads share 1 address space. 10 processes each have their own copy.
3. **Communication**: Threads share heap memory directly — no IPC overhead. Processes need pipes, sockets, or shared memory.
4. **Context switch speed**: Thread switches within the same process don't require TLB flush (same page table).

**Danger**: Since threads share memory, concurrent access to shared variables without synchronization causes race conditions, data corruption, and bugs that are extremely hard to reproduce and debug.
topics.real_world_analogy: A process is like an apartment. A thread is a person living in that apartment. Multiple people (threads) share the kitchen, living room, and bathroom (shared memory). But each person has their own bedroom and personal diary (private stack and registers). If two people try to use the kitchen stove at the same time without coordination (no synchronization), food gets burned (race condition).
why_it_exists: Web servers handle 10,000+ concurrent connections — creating a process per connection is too expensive.
GUI applications need threads: one thread renders the UI, another handles button clicks, another downloads data in the background.
Modern CPUs have 8-16 cores — threads are how applications utilize all cores simultaneously.
tech_world: Java's `Thread` class and `ExecutorService` for managed thread pools.
Python's `threading` module creates threads, but the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) prevents true parallel CPU execution.
Go's goroutines are lightweight green threads multiplexed onto OS threads by the Go runtime.
Nginx uses a fixed pool of worker threads per worker process for handling thousands of concurrent requests.
key_points: Thread = lightweight execution unit within a process.
Shared: code, data, heap, file descriptors, PID. Private: stack, registers, PC, TID.
Faster creation and context switching than processes.
Communication via shared memory (no IPC needed) — but requires synchronization.
Race condition: Two threads read-modify-write a shared variable simultaneously → corrupted state.
interview_focus: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
What are the advantages of multi-threading?

interview_questions.question: What is the difference between a Process and a Thread?
interview_questions.answer:
| Aspect | Process | Thread |
|--------|---------|--------|
| Definition | Independent program in execution | Lightweight execution unit within a process |
| Memory | Own address space (code, data, heap, stack) | Shares process address space; own stack only |
| Creation cost | Expensive (copy address space, even with COW) | Cheap (share existing address space) |
| Context switch | Expensive (TLB flush, page table switch) | Cheap (same address space, no TLB flush) |
| Communication | IPC required (pipes, sockets, shared memory) | Direct shared memory access |
| Crash impact | One process crash doesn't affect others | One thread crash can kill the entire process |
| Isolation | Strong (separate address spaces) | Weak (shared memory) |

Use processes when you need isolation and fault tolerance (Chrome tabs). Use threads when you need high-performance concurrency with shared state (web server request handling).

topics.title: User Threads vs Kernel Threads
topics.what_is_it: User threads are managed entirely by a user-space threading library (invisible to the OS kernel). Kernel threads are managed directly by the OS kernel and are individually schedulable by the kernel scheduler.
topics.simple_explanation:
**User Threads (Green Threads):**
- Managed by a user-space library (e.g., old Java green threads, GNU Pth).
- Kernel sees only ONE process — it has NO idea multiple threads exist inside.
- Thread creation, switching, and synchronization happen in user-space (no system call needed → very fast).
- **Fatal flaw**: If one user thread makes a blocking syscall (e.g., `read()`), the ENTIRE process blocks — because the kernel sees it as one process. All other user threads stop.
- **No multicore parallelism**: Kernel schedules the process on ONE core — user threads run sequentially even on a 16-core CPU.

**Kernel Threads:**
- Each thread is known to and managed by the kernel (each has its own `task_struct` in Linux).
- Kernel schedules each thread independently on any available CPU core.
- If one thread blocks on I/O, the kernel schedules another thread from the same process — no deadlock.
- Thread creation requires a system call (`clone()` on Linux) → slower than user-space thread creation.

**Modern approach**: Most languages use kernel threads. Go uses a hybrid: M:N threading where M goroutines (user threads) are multiplexed onto N kernel threads by the Go runtime scheduler.
topics.real_world_analogy: User threads are like employees in a single-desk shared coworking space — the building manager (kernel) sees one desk (one process), so all employees must take turns at that one desk. Kernel threads are like employees with their own desks — the building manager knows each person and can assign them to different rooms (CPU cores) independently.
why_it_exists: User threads were designed when OS kernels couldn't efficiently manage thousands of threads — user-space scheduling avoided kernel overhead.
Kernel threads became dominant when modern OS kernels optimized thread management with O(1) schedulers and efficient clone() syscalls.
Go's goroutines revived the M:N model by implementing a sophisticated user-space scheduler on top of kernel threads.
tech_world: Linux uses kernel threads exclusively — `pthread_create()` calls `clone()` syscall internally.
Go runtime schedules millions of goroutines (user threads) onto a small pool of OS kernel threads (GOMAXPROCS).
Java switched from green threads to native kernel threads in Java 1.3. Project Loom (Java 21+) re-introduces virtual threads (user-space) on top of platform threads (kernel).
Python's threads are kernel threads, but the GIL serializes their execution on a single core.
key_points: User Threads: Managed in user-space. Fast creation. No kernel awareness. One blocking call blocks all threads. No multicore parallelism.
Kernel Threads: Managed by OS. Each independently scheduled on CPU cores. Blocking one doesn't affect others. Slightly slower creation.
Modern standard: Kernel threads (pthreads on Linux, Win32 threads on Windows).
M:N model (Go goroutines, Java virtual threads): M user threads multiplexed onto N kernel threads — best of both worlds.
interview_focus: What is the difference between user-level and kernel-level threads?
Why can't user-level threads achieve true parallelism?

interview_questions.question: What is the difference between User-Level Threads and Kernel-Level Threads?
interview_questions.answer:
**User-Level Threads**: Created and managed by a user-space library without kernel involvement. The kernel sees only one schedulable entity (the process). Advantages: Ultra-fast creation and switching (no syscalls). Disadvantages: (1) One blocking I/O call freezes ALL threads. (2) Cannot utilize multiple CPU cores — kernel assigns the process to one core.

**Kernel-Level Threads**: Each thread has its own kernel task_struct and is independently scheduled by the kernel. Advantages: (1) True multicore parallelism. (2) One thread blocking doesn't affect others. Disadvantages: Thread creation/switching involves syscalls (slightly slower).

**Modern solution**: Go's goroutines use M:N threading — millions of lightweight goroutines (user-level) multiplexed onto a pool of OS kernel threads. This gets the performance of user threads with the parallelism of kernel threads.

topics.title: Multithreading Models (1:1, M:1, M:N)
topics.what_is_it: Three models for mapping user-level threads to kernel threads: Many-to-One (M:1), One-to-One (1:1), and Many-to-Many (M:N). The choice determines parallelism capability and scheduling efficiency.
topics.simple_explanation:
**Many-to-One (M:1):**
- Many user threads → 1 kernel thread.
- Entire process gets ONE CPU core. No parallelism.
- One blocking call blocks everyone.
- Example: Old Solaris Green Threads.

**One-to-One (1:1):**
- Each user thread → 1 kernel thread.
- True parallelism — each thread scheduled independently on any core.
- Downside: Creating 10,000 threads means 10,000 kernel threads — high memory overhead (~8MB stack per thread).
- Example: Linux pthreads, Windows threads, Java native threads.

**Many-to-Many (M:N):**
- M user threads multiplexed onto N kernel threads (M >> N).
- Runtime scheduler decides which user thread runs on which kernel thread.
- Best of both worlds: lightweight creation (user-space) + multicore parallelism (kernel threads).
- Most complex to implement correctly.
- Example: Go goroutines (millions of goroutines on GOMAXPROCS kernel threads), Erlang BEAM VM, Java Virtual Threads.
topics.real_world_analogy: M:1 is one cashier serving a line of 100 customers — slow, sequential. 1:1 is hiring a dedicated cashier for every customer — fast but expensive. M:N is having 4 cashiers and 100 customers with a smart queue manager directing customers to available cashiers — efficient use of resources.
why_it_exists: M:1 was used when kernel threads were expensive (old Unix systems with no lightweight thread support).
1:1 is the most straightforward and widely used today — modern kernels handle thousands of threads efficiently.
M:N is used when applications need millions of concurrent tasks (Go web servers handling 1M goroutines on 8 OS threads).
tech_world: Linux + pthreads = 1:1 model. Each pthread maps to exactly one kernel task_struct.
Go runtime = M:N model. GOMAXPROCS (default = number of CPU cores) kernel threads serve millions of goroutines.
Java Virtual Threads (Project Loom, Java 21+) = M:N model. Lightweight virtual threads scheduled onto platform (carrier) threads.
Nginx = 1:1 model with event loop — small number of worker threads each handling thousands of connections via epoll.
key_points: M:1 (Many-to-One): All user threads → 1 kernel thread. No parallelism. Obsolete.
1:1 (One-to-One): Each user thread = 1 kernel thread. Full parallelism. Most common today (pthreads, Java).
M:N (Many-to-Many): M user threads on N kernel threads. Best scalability. Complex runtime (Go, Erlang, Java 21+).
1:1 limitation: 10,000 threads × 8MB stack = 80GB memory. Impractical for C10K problem.
M:N solution: Go handles 1 million goroutines with only 8-16 kernel threads using 2-8KB stacks per goroutine.
interview_focus: Compare the three multithreading models with examples.
Why does Go use the M:N model instead of 1:1?

interview_questions.question: Why does Go use the M:N threading model instead of creating one OS thread per goroutine?
interview_questions.answer:
If Go used 1:1 threading, creating 1 million goroutines would require 1 million OS kernel threads. Each kernel thread needs ~8MB default stack → 8TB of memory (impossible). Plus, the OS scheduler would collapse trying to schedule 1M threads.

Go's M:N model solves this:
1. **Tiny stacks**: Goroutines start with 2-8KB stacks that grow dynamically. 1M goroutines = ~8GB.
2. **User-space scheduling**: Go's runtime scheduler (GMP model: Goroutines, Machine threads, Processors) multiplexes goroutines onto GOMAXPROCS OS threads.
3. **Non-blocking I/O**: When a goroutine blocks on I/O, the runtime parks it and schedules another goroutine on the same OS thread — no wasted threads.
4. **Work stealing**: Idle OS threads steal goroutines from busy threads' run queues for load balancing.

sections.title: 05 CPU Scheduling Algorithms
sections.description: Master CPU scheduling policies: FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Round Robin, Priority, and MLFQ with their trade-offs.

topics.title: CPU Scheduling Fundamentals
topics.what_is_it: CPU scheduling is the OS mechanism that decides WHICH ready process/thread gets to execute on the CPU, and for HOW LONG. The scheduler's goal is to maximize CPU utilization, throughput, and fairness while minimizing waiting time and response time.
topics.simple_explanation:
When 20 processes are in the Ready queue but only 4 CPU cores are available, the **CPU scheduler** decides:
1. **Which process runs next?** (selection algorithm)
2. **How long does it run?** (time quantum / preemption policy)

**Key Metrics:**
- **CPU Utilization**: Percentage of time CPU is doing useful work (target: >90%).
- **Throughput**: Number of processes completed per unit time.
- **Turnaround Time**: Total time from process arrival to completion (wait + execution).
